content: Chlorodyne was one of the most renowned patent medicines sold in the British Isles. It was developed in the 19th century by Dr. J. Collis Browne, a physician serving in the British Indian Army. Initially, it was formulated for the treatment of cholera. Dr. Browne later sold the formula to a pharmacist named Davenport, who extensively marketed it as a remedy for various conditions, including cholera, diarrhea, insomnia, neuralgia, and migraines. The primary ingredients of Chlorodyne included laudanum (an alcoholic solution of opium), tincture of cannabis, and chloroform. These components made it highly effective in alleviating pain, acting as a sedative, and treating diarrhea. Chlorodyne achieved significant commercial success for many years. Due to the well-known nature of its active ingredients, local chemists often prepared and sold cheaper, generic versions of the medicine. For example, the 21st edition of H. Douthwaite's text (1932) described a formula called Tinctura Chloroformi et Morphinæ Composita, which was intended to mimic the proprietary medicine Chlorodyne. This imitation formula included chloroform, tincture of capsicum, tincture of Indian hemp, oil of peppermint, glycerin, alcohol, morphine hydrochloride, and diluted hydrocyanic acid. In addition to generic versions, several rival sellers marketed their own branded formulations of Chlorodyne, such as Freeman's, Teasdale's, and Towle's. The authenticity of these competing brands was often a subject of heated disputes, as evidenced by historical advertisements and illustrations. Despite its effectiveness, Chlorodyne's high opiate content rendered it highly addictive. Overdoses, whether accidental or intentional, became a common occurrence. Coroner's reports from such cases frequently described the deceased being found in rooms littered with empty Chlorodyne bottles. Throughout the 20th century, the formulation of Chlorodyne underwent significant changes. Cannabis was removed from the mixture, and the opiate content was progressively reduced. Today, the legacy of Dr. Collis Browne persists in Britain through a product sold under the trade name J Collis Browne's Mixture, which is used for the relief of coughs and diarrhea. This modern formulation contains morphine and peppermint oil.
